@AndersBroman that's an example of a merge request containing 2 commits that MUST NOT be sqashed.
Ok, staying out of reviews.

No please :(

Personally I find the Gitlab GUI a bit confusing. When you look at the changes tab, it displays all the changes without the ability to see separate commits (or I missed the way to achieve this). It seems like the right was to do it in that case is to click on each commit and then you get the changes of a single commit (which is cumbersome).

Some people are purposely sending one MR with several separate commits (like you did). I'm not sure this is a good idea as we need multiple clicks to see the changes that can be unrelated (as what happened here) and could have been done in separate MRs.

But we have several examples of people not familiar with Git / Gitlab that where pushing new commits following the code review instead of amending their initial change (despite our documentation asking to amend). For those we must squash the commits to avoid merging something that does not even compile and would break bisection.

Like @AndersBroman I prefer having a separate MR per change as it is less error prone / less heavy for the reviewer. But maybe that's simply because of a lack of practice on my side.

Guys, I can get that switching from a code review system to another can be harsh. We need to find the way to work at best, without too much pain: we're developers, after all.

I am used to gitlab, since it's our internal CRS, but despite that I am still getting confused sometimes when working on wireshark. Conventions are above the CRS: different projects on the same CRS can require completely different workflows.

On gerrit we asked people A LOT OF TIMES to split their commits into smaller ones: for easier review and to stick on a topic. Gerrit helped on this: one page, one commit, one linear comments flow, etc. However think on how many times we referred to a comment on a previous revision that was, actually, superseded. We had to explain a million of times to the users how to amend, etc... basically how things worked. People are much more used to fork/merge model (it is github's) than to Gerrit's. WE were more used to Gerrit (just to develop Wireshark, actually, at least in my case). Have you ever tried to push a change to the Linux kernel? Or to any project using absurd-proprietary-never-seen workflows? Did they change their workflow because I didn't get it? No: I had to adapt. People contributing to wireshark will have to do the same. What is required our side is to give clear and short instruction we stick to.

That said: the merge requests with multiple commits have the advantage that you may find something to fix (e.g. a bug) when doing something totally different. Pushing 2 MRs will result in a slower workflow because one MR will require another to be merged first. This MR is an example of that. When merging multiple files into one, I find a bug in a CI script, and I fixed it. The MR stayed consistent with its 2 commits. The drawback is that, as Pascal said, reviewing commits one by one requires to go to "commits" tab, click on one and so on, that is slow. Moreover, commenting on commit messages is even worse.

Since each project has its own peculiarity, I would also be fine with having one commit per MR. But in this case that would need to be enforced by a CI job that prevents having MR with more than one commit (see !1480 for something I am working on). If we want to go this way I guess we should discuss it with Gerald on the -core ML.

@AndersBroman don't give up: you did and still doing a great job. We will work together to find the best way to have fun.
